Dear Hiring Manager,

I am applying for the Senior Data Analyst role on your marketplace analytics team. For the past five years, I worked at Fernwood, a regional grocery delivery company with about 300 employees, first as a data analyst and then as the lead analyst for pricing and promotions. Fernwood was small enough that I worked directly with the operations, finance and marketing teams, and I learned how to turn messy data into decisions that people actually use.

My main project in the last two years was a new model for promotional pricing. Before this project, the marketing team planned discounts based on what worked the year before, and nobody measured the real effect of a promotion after it ended. I built a simple test-and-control framework that compared stores with and without each promotion, and I set up a weekly report that showed the extra revenue, the cost of the discount and the effect on basket size. In the first year, we stopped about a third of the promotions because they lost money, and gross margin went up by 1.8 points.

I also rebuilt our core reporting. When I joined, most reports were Excel files that three people updated by hand every Monday. I moved the data into a warehouse, wrote the transformations in SQL and dbt, and built dashboards in Looker for the main teams. The Monday reporting work went from about 12 hours per week to less than one, and the numbers became consistent across teams for the first time.

I enjoy the technical work, but I think my strongest skill is communication. I spend a lot of time on how to present results so that a store manager or a CFO can understand them in two minutes. I write short summaries with one clear recommendation, and I always include what the data cannot tell us. In my experience, people trust an analysis more when the analyst is honest about its limits.

Your job posting mentions three things that match my experience closely. First, you want someone to own experimentation for the seller tools. I designed and analyzed more than 60 experiments in my current role, from price tests to changes in the delivery fee, and I know the common problems, such as small sample sizes, novelty effects and tests that end too early. Second, you mention a need to improve data quality. I built automated checks that caught broken data feeds before they reached the dashboards, and I wrote the documentation that new analysts on my team still use. Third, you want an analyst who can mentor others. For the last two years, I managed two junior analysts and ran a weekly SQL class for anyone in the company who wanted to learn.

I am especially interested in your company because of the size and complexity of a two-sided marketplace. In grocery delivery, I mostly studied one side, the customer. The chance to work on problems where sellers and buyers affect each other, such as search ranking, fees and seller quality, is exactly the kind of challenge I want next.

This guide covers your first two weeks on the team. Keep it open during your first days, and come back to it when you have questions. Your manager will go through the most important parts with you on day one.

Week 1: Accounts and tools
On your first morning, IT will give you a laptop and your login details. Please set up two-factor authentication before you do anything else. You will need it for the email system, the CRM, the help desk and the internal wiki. If the setup does not work, call the IT help desk at extension 4410.

During the first week, you will get access to these tools:
- Zendesk, for customer tickets. You will start with read-only access and get full access after your training on Wednesday.
- Salesforce, for account information and renewal dates.
- Gong, for recorded customer calls. Listen to at least five calls before your first shadow session.
- Slack, for team chat. Join the channels #cs-team, #cs-escalations and #product-updates.

On Tuesday and Wednesday, you will attend product training with the other new hires from sales and support. The trainers are Olivia Brandt and Kenji Mori. They will show you the main features of the product and the most common customer problems. Bring your questions, because there is time for them at the end of each session.

On Thursday, you will shadow a senior Customer Success Manager for the full day. You will join their calls, see how they prepare for a quarterly business review and watch how they handle a difficult conversation. Take notes and write down anything that is not clear.

Week 2: First accounts
In your second week, you will get a starter book of about 15 small accounts. These accounts are stable, with renewal dates at least six months away, so you have time to learn without too much pressure. Your manager will choose them for you and introduce you to each customer by email.

For each account, please do the following in your first two weeks:
1. Read the account history in Salesforce, including the notes from the previous owner.
2. Check the open tickets in Zendesk and the health score in the CS dashboard.
3. Send a short introduction email to the main contact.
4. Book a 30-minute call to understand their goals for the next six months.

Our main metrics are gross retention, net retention and the customer health score. The team target for this year is 92 percent gross retention and 108 percent net retention. You will not be measured on these numbers in your first 90 days, but you should understand how your work affects them.

How we work
We answer every customer email within one business day, even if the answer is only that we are looking into the question. When a customer is unhappy, we call them instead of writing a long email. Team meetings happen every Monday at 10 am. We review renewals for the next 60 days, share wins and talk about difficult accounts. Every other Thursday, we have a learning session where one person on the team presents a topic, such as a new feature or a good customer story.

Who to ask
Your manager is your first contact for questions about your accounts, your goals and your schedule. window_title: Write a review - Northfield ProBlend 900 - Google Chrome
before:
I bought this blender in March to replace an old one that finally died after eight years. I did a lot of research first and compared it with two other models in the same price range. After about seven months of almost daily use, I have a clear opinion, so here is my long review for anyone who is still deciding.

What I use it for
Mostly smoothies in the morning, with frozen fruit, spinach, oats and peanut butter. About twice a week I also make soup, hummus or a sauce. My partner uses it for protein shakes after the gym. Once or twice a month I use it to grind coffee beans or make oat flour.

Power and results
This is where the blender is excellent. Frozen fruit and ice are not a problem at all. A full jar of smoothie with frozen mango, banana and kale takes about 45 seconds on high, and the result is completely smooth, with no chunks of ice and no leaf bits. My old blender needed me to stop and stir every few seconds. With this one, I use the tamper once at the start, and that is it.

Hot soup works well too. The manual says you can blend hot liquids if the lid is locked and you start on low, and I have done this many times with no problem. Hummus comes out very smooth, smoother than the store-bought kind. The only thing it does not do well is a small amount of anything. If you want to blend one cup of sauce, the blades spin under the food and you have to scrape the sides a lot. The company sells a smaller jar for this, but it costs 60 dollars, which I think is too much.

Noise
It is loud. Not louder than my old blender, but not quiet either. On high, it is about as loud as a hair dryer. My partner leaves for work at 6 am, and I can blend without waking up the kids if I close the kitchen door, but you would not want to use it in an open apartment while someone sleeps.

Cleaning
Very easy. I fill the jar halfway with warm water and a drop of dish soap, run it on high for 30 seconds, and rinse. The jar is not dishwasher safe according to the manual, which surprised me at this price, but the self-clean trick works so well that I do not miss the dishwasher.

Build quality and design
The base is heavy and does not move on the counter, even on high. The jar is clear and thick, and after seven months it still looks new, with no scratches or cloudy spots. The dial and the switches feel solid. The cord is a little short, about three feet, so think about where your outlet is. The jar is tall, and with the lid on, it does not fit under our upper cabinets. I keep it on the counter with the jar next to the base.

Customer service
In May, the lid started to leak at the edge. I contacted support on a Sunday, and they replied the next morning. They sent a new lid gasket for free, and it arrived in four days. The new gasket fixed the leak completely.

Price
It is expensive. I paid 449 dollars on sale. For that much money, I expected a dishwasher-safe jar and maybe the small jar in the box. But it replaced my blender, my food processor for most tasks, and my coffee grinder, and I expect it to last at least as long as my old one.

Guía de incorporación al laboratorio
Vendimia 2026

Bienvenidos al laboratorio de la bodega. Antes de nada, una norma que no tiene excepciones: aquí la densidad del mosto se mide siempre con el picnómetro, nunca con el densímetro de flotación ni con el refractómetro de mano. Sabemos que en muchas bodegas se usa el densímetro porque es más rápido, pero el picnómetro nos da la precisión que necesitamos para decidir el momento del descube, y así los datos de todos los turnos son comparables.

Esta guía resume lo que necesitáis saber durante vuestras primeras semanas. Leedla entera antes de vuestro primer turno y tenedla siempre a mano, porque durante la vendimia no siempre habrá alguien libre para resolver dudas.

1. Horarios y turnos

Durante la vendimia hay dos turnos: de 7:00 a 15:00 y de 15:00 a 23:00. Los cambios de turno se piden a Begoña, la jefa de laboratorio, con al menos 48 horas de antelación. Los fines de semana trabaja una sola persona por turno, así que el trabajo tiene que quedar al día antes del viernes.

2. Seguridad

Es obligatorio usar bata, gafas y guantes de nitrilo en todo momento. Los reactivos ácidos se guardan en el armario ventilado de la izquierda y nunca se dejan sobre la mesa. Si se derrama hidróxido sódico, usad el kit de neutralización que está junto a la ducha de emergencia y avisad a Begoña, aunque parezca poca cosa. En la sala de depósitos, durante la fermentación, se acumula CO2: no entréis nunca solos y llevad siempre el detector portátil encendido.

3. Recepción de la uva

Cada remolque que llega a la báscula se muestrea antes de descargar. Se toman tres muestras de distintas zonas del remolque con la sonda, se mezclan en un cubo y se mide el grado probable en la propia báscula. Ese dato solo sirve para clasificar la uva y para pagar al viticultor, no para el seguimiento de la fermentación. Anotad el número de remolque, la parcela, la variedad y el grado en la hoja de recepción.

4. Análisis de rutina

Cada mosto que entra en un depósito se analiza el mismo día: acidez total, pH, ácido málico y nitrógeno fácilmente asimilable. Los resultados se cargan en la hoja compartida antes de terminar el turno. Si el nitrógeno sale por debajo de 150 mg/l, avisad al enólogo, Javier Sáenz, porque probablemente habrá que añadir nutrientes.

5. Etiquetado de muestras

Toda muestra que entra en el laboratorio lleva una etiqueta con el número de depósito, la fecha, la hora y vuestras iniciales. Las muestras sin etiqueta se tiran, sin excepción. Las que hay que guardar para un segundo análisis se conservan en la nevera pequeña durante quince días, en la balda que corresponde a cada semana.

6. Limpieza del material

Todo el material de vidrio se lava con agua destilada al terminar cada análisis y se deja secar boca abajo en el escurridor. Las pipetas automáticas se calibran cada lunes y el resultado se anota en el registro de calibración. Si una pipeta da un error mayor del 1 %, se retira y se etiqueta como «fuera de uso» hasta que la revise el técnico.

7. Control de fermentación

Este es el trabajo más importante de la vendimia y también el que más errores provoca cuando alguien llega nuevo. Cada mañana, antes de las nueve, tomad una muestra de cada depósito en fermentación con el grifo de muestreo, después de dejar correr un poco de mosto para limpiar el conducto. Medid la temperatura con la sonda del propio depósito y anotadla en la ficha que cuelga de la escalera. Si un depósito pasa de 28 °C, abrid el circuito de frío y avisad a Javier.
